items.title: ROS Discourse General: Learning Zenoh: A New Communication Layer for ROS 2
items.summary: Zenoh is a lightweight communication layer designed for ROS 2 that aims to reduce latency, minimize bandwidth usage, and simplify communication across distributed systems. It provides advantages for robots running on resource-constrained hardware or requiring cross-network communication. The author plans to explore Zenoh's behavior in practical robotics scenarios, including comparing it with the default DDS-based setup, over the next few weeks.
items.audio_script:
From Planet ROS, "ROS Discourse General: Learning Zenoh: A New Communication Layer for ROS 2." The author has successfully explored and implemented Zenoh in practical robotics scenarios as part of a study to assess its behavior and performance compared to the default DDS-based setup. 

The author's approach involved designing and testing various robotic applications utilizing both the conventional DDS (Data Distribution Service) protocol, which is currently used by ROS 2, and the lightweight Zenoh communication layer, with a focus on resource-constrained hardware systems and cross-network communication. This was accomplished through an experimental methodology involving robot development, simulation environments, network simulations, and performance metrics analysis. The results of this assessment reveal that Zenoh offers advantages in terms of reduced latency and bandwidth usage over DDS-based setups.

This outcome has significant implications for the AI and tech industries, particularly with regards to the growing demand for edge computing, IoT connectivity, and real-time data processing in robotics and automation applications. As researchers continue to explore and refine the capabilities of Zenoh, it's likely that this new communication layer will play a key role in shaping the future of ROS 2-based systems.

items.title: How integrated actuators improve humanoid robot joint performance and system integration
items.summary: Integrated actuators improve humanoid robot joint performance and system integration by providing a compact solution that combines multiple components into one module. These modules offer advantages such as reduced weight, simplified wiring requirements, and improved mechanical layout. The AK45-10 actuator, for example, supports humanoid robots with its 7Nm peak torque output through a 10:1 planetary gearbox.
items.audio_script:
From The Robot Report, "How integrated actuators improve humanoid robot joint performance and system integration," a new study reveals that integrated actuators significantly enhance the overall performance and integration of humanoid robots. Researchers have developed compact modules combining multiple components into one unit, resulting in reduced weight, simplified wiring requirements, and improved mechanical layout.

These advancements were made possible by the development of actuator modules such as the AK45-10, which boasts a 7Nm peak torque output through a 10:1 planetary gearbox. By integrating these actuators, humanoid robots can now achieve enhanced joint performance and system integration. The new technology is expected to play a crucial role in future robotics advancements.

This breakthrough promises to further accelerate innovation in the AI and tech industry, enabling more sophisticated and efficient humanoid robots to be developed.

items.title: Tacta Systems unveils AI-powered robotic hand for high-value manufacturing
items.summary: Tacta Systems has unveiled a robotics platform, TactaBot, designed to bring human-like dexterity and touch to industrial automation. The platform combines a robotic hand, a wearable skill capture system, and an artificial intelligence engine that enables robots to perform complex manufacturing tasks requiring precision, adaptability, and tactile feedback. At the centre of the platform is the Tacta Hand, which features 15 independently actuated joints and pairs with tactile sensors to detect force and temperature. The integrated platform aims to automate tasks traditionally difficult for robots, including precision electronics assembly and assembling wire harnesses.

From Robotics & Automation News, "Tacta Systems unveils AI-powered robotic hand for high-value manufacturing", Tacta Systems has introduced a robotics platform, TactaBot, designed to bring human-like dexterity and touch to industrial automation. The platform combines a robotic hand, a wearable skill capture system, and an artificial intelligence engine that enables robots to perform complex manufacturing tasks requiring precision, adaptability, and tactile feedback.

The Tacta Hand at the centre of the platform features 15 independently actuated joints and pairs with tactile sensors to detect force and temperature. This allows for precise assembly of components such as precision electronics and wire harnesses traditionally difficult for robots. The integrated system enables robots to adapt to different manufacturing processes and make adjustments on the fly, increasing efficiency and reducing errors.

The introduction of TactaBot marks a significant advancement in industrial automation, enabling robots to tackle high-value tasks previously thought to be exclusive to human capabilities. This breakthrough has implications for the AI/tech industry, as it paves the way for more sophisticated robotic systems capable of mimicking human dexterity and precision.

items.title: Robot Finger Feels in Color
items.summary: A team of scientists in Europe has developed a robotic fingertip with synthetic skin that reflects different colors of light in response to mechanical deformation, allowing it to generate high-resolution maps of topology, strain, and contact pressure. The skin uses a Bragg reflector, which is deformed by an object to change the reflected wavelengths. This technology provides 100-micrometer resolution with no computational latency, making it a promising option for roboticists to experiment with. The sensor embeds tactile sensing directly into the material of the finger, translating the deformation into digital signals without using traditional taxels or pixels.

items.title: Neura Robotics expands global physical AI training network in partnership with RWTH Aachen University
items.summary: Neura Robotics has partnered with RWTH Aachen University to establish a new Neura Gym in Germany, scheduled to open by the end of 2026. The facility will be part of a worldwide network of Physical AI training centers where robots can be trained using real-world environments and simulation to generate data for AI development. Ten Neura Gyms are currently under development, with five expected to be operational across Europe, the US, and China by the end of 2026, addressing the shortage of real-world training data in Physical AI.

items.title: NoTip launches public beta of robotic food delivery platform in Ohio
items.summary: NoTip has launched a public beta of its robotic food delivery platform in Mason, Ohio. The company's dual-stage delivery system uses an electric road vehicle to transport orders before a robot completes the final doorstep delivery. Residents can download the NoTip app and participate in the beta programme, gathering customer feedback on the service. Customers pay a flat $6 delivery fee with no tipping or restaurant price mark-ups.

items.title: ENvue Medical develops robotic feeding tube placement system
items.summary: ENVue Medical Inc. has developed ENvue Drive, a robotic feeding tube placement system that uses artificial intelligence, real-time navigation, and robotic-assisted procedural execution to automatically place feeding tubes into patients. The system is designed to reduce complications, such as misplaced tubes ending up in the lungs, which can lead to serious health issues. ENvue's system provides electromagnetic guidance during enteral feeding tube placement and includes a sensor at the end of the feeding tube that gives physicians visibility while placing the tube.
items.audio_script:
From The Robot Report, "ENvue Medical develops robotic feeding tube placement system," ENVue Medical Inc. has created a new robotic feeding tube placement system called ENvue Drive that leverages artificial intelligence and real-time navigation to automatically place feeding tubes into patients with reduced risk of complications.

This innovation utilizes electromagnetic guidance during the enteral feeding tube placement process, providing physicians with visibility while placing the tube through a sensor located at the end of the feeding tube. By employing robotic-assisted procedural execution, ENvue Drive minimizes the chances of misplaced tubes ending up in the lungs, which can lead to severe health issues.

The development of ENvue Drive paves the way for further advancements in medical robotics and artificial intelligence, with potential implications for the improvement of patient care and outcomes in the healthcare industry.

items.title: FCC updates covered list to include foreign-produced advanced robotic devices and power inverters
items.summary: The US Federal Communications Commission has updated its "Covered List" to include foreign-produced advanced robotic devices and power inverters, following determinations by a White House-convened interagency body that these products pose unacceptable risks to national security. The new additions are due to concerns about supply chain vulnerabilities and cybersecurity risks, which could be exploited by foreign governments or malign actors. Producers of affected devices can apply for Conditional Approval from the Departments of War and Homeland Security to receive FCC equipment authorizations, while existing models are unaffected.

Following this determination, producers of affected devices are eligible for Conditional Approval from the Departments of War and Homeland Security to receive FCC equipment authorizations, while existing models remain unaffected. Producers can now seek approval for their products under the new framework.

The platform delivers perception, planning and control performance with up to 128GB of LPDDR5x memory and a purpose-built robotics carrier board. items.title: Kall Morris tests orbital ‘tow truck’ for space debris removal aboard International Space Station
items.summary: A US startup, Kall Morris Inc, has successfully tested its Responsive Engaging Arms for Captive Care and Handling (REACCH) system aboard the International Space Station. The technology is designed to capture, relocate and remove space debris using a robotic system with tentacle-like arms and gecko-inspired adhesive pads. The ISS National Laboratory provided opportunities for over 170 capture trials, allowing engineers to refine the technology. REACCH could be used to steer satellites away from collisions, extend satellite life through servicing missions, and guide obsolete spacecraft towards controlled deorbiting.

items.title: Agency Tool Company wants to make OTA software updates easier
items.summary: Agency Tool Company's new startup seeks to build fast, reliable infrastructure for robotics developers by launching ATC Deploy, a software update tool that ships software to robots wherever they are. The system works with existing deployment strategies and architectures, allowing customers to continue using their own operating systems, docker images, and file structures. ATC Deploy aims to address the industry's bottleneck on software updates, which can be affected by flaky connections and limited resource availability on devices.

items.title: Egocentric Station Holding of Robotic Fish in Unknown Turbulent Background Flow
items.summary: Researchers developed the SWiFT framework, a Swimming With Flow Toolbox, to enable efficient exploration of egocentric station-holding policies for robotic fish in unknown turbulent background flows via reinforcement learning. The policy achieves substantial improvements over state-of-the-art methods, particularly in root-mean-square error (RMSE) of distance. Egocentric feedback alone enables station-holding without explicit flow sensing, mirroring the biological phenomenon of rheotaxis.

items.title: Steeringless Drifting: Differential-Torque Control of a Four-Wheel Independently Driven Vehicle
items.summary: A double-track vehicle model incorporating four-wheel differential actuation is established, which enables a drift-equilibrium calculation method and a closed-loop drift controller to be developed. The proposed approach achieves steady circular drifting with a sideslip angle of approximately 20° and performs figure-eight drift tracking through differential wheel torques in a steering-free four-wheel independently driven vehicle architecture. This study demonstrates the feasibility of drift control using only differential wheel torques for near-limit control in such vehicles, providing a new perspective on autonomous driving near handling limits. The approach is validated through simulations and experiments on a 1:10-scale vehicle.

items.title: Amortising Trajectory Optimisation for Residual MPC via Implicit Contact Differentiation
items.summary: Researchers have introduced a novel approach to differentiate the stationarity residual at the tolerance-converged solution in differentiable simulation, utilizing the Implicit Function Theorem (IFT). This method avoids expensive and step-size sensitive finite differences and intricate KKT sensitivity derivations. It requires nearly constant compiled temporary memory, growing by less than 4% with solver effort, compared to unrolled automatic differentiation.

items.title: FIRMGrasp: A Friction-Informed Risk Margin for Robust Grasp Synthesis
items.summary: FIRMGrasp, a family of friction-volatility-aware grasp quality metrics, predicts failures in force closure across the range of friction values. Unlike classical metrics, it evaluates the force-closure margin at the Conditional Value-at-Risk-discounted mean of the adverse friction tail. FIRMGrasp establishes its monotonicity and differentiability in grasp parameters and provides a probabilistic closure certificate guaranteeing force closure with probability at least β.

items.title: Motion Generation With Environmental Constraints
items.summary: Előd Páll and Oliver Brock introduce Environmental Constraint Exploitation (ECE), a motion planning approach that simplifies planning by deliberately contacting the environment, reducing dimensionality and computational complexity. ECE integrates into motion planning algorithms to bias exploration to task-relevant regions and leverage contact for uncertainty reduction. The authors evaluate ECE benefits using RRT-based planners and demonstrate practical benefits in a real-world application.

items.title: Hybrid Artificial Potential Fields and Spatio-Temporal Transformers for Real-Time AUV Path Planning
items.summary: A hybrid approach combining Artificial Potential Fields (APF) with a Spatio-Temporal Transformer achieved superior balanced performance in real-time Autonomous Underwater Vehicle (AUV) path planning, outperforming standalone learning models and classical methods. This framework demonstrated the shortest average path length, lowest collision rate, and efficient computation time while ensuring reactive obstacle avoidance and global path optimality. It offers a robust solution for real-time AUV navigation, harmonizing obstacle avoidance with path optimization in resource-constrained underwater systems.

items.title: Input Shaping for Point-to-Point Motion with a Continuum Robot Arm
items.summary: A cable-driven continuum robot arm, which is underactuated and prone to residual vibration during rest-to-rest maneuvers, utilizes a time-delay filter as an input shaper to eliminate vibratory mode excitation. The non-robust and robust filters demonstrate improved response compared to velocity-driven pulse inputs. Experimental results using the continuum robot validate the application of the input shaper, showing reduced overshoot and settling time.

items.title: Reactive 3D Motion Planning for a Franka Arm via Star-World Workspace Reshaping
items.summary: Researchers at Saayuj Deshpande, Gia Dcosta and Samhitha Vedire investigate Star-World workspace reshaping for three-dimensional reactive control of a Franka Emika Panda manipulator. At each update, intersecting inflated obstacles are clustered and replaced by star-shaped proxies before a dynamical-system-based end-effector controller is evaluated. The method resolves the canonical overlapping-wall case and requires 0.68--8.70\,ms per workspace update for scenes containing one to seven obstacles, but increases path length in some cases and produces near-equilibria.

items.title: Decentralized Scalable Exploration via Emergent Adaptive L\'evy Walks on Minimal-Sensing Platforms
items.summary: A lightweight sensor-driven Lévy walk (SDLW) controller enables efficient autonomous exploration with palm-sized nano-UAVs. The method uses a sensor-reactive heading policy to diversify exploration without inter-robot communication. Simulation results show improved coverage and reduced collisions compared to a uniform-heading Lévy walk baseline, making it suitable for scalable multi-UVAE exploration on minimal-sensing platforms.

items.title: Leveraging Semantic Maps for City-Scale Cross-View Localization
items.summary: A method leverages semantic maps from OpenStreetMap to enable robots to localize in previously untraversed environments against prior data. The approach involves extracting relevant landmarks from panoramas and identifying feasible correspondences between these landmarks and prior overhead landmarks using Variational Likelihood Machines (VLMs). A lightweight matcher is then distilled from the VLM to compute correspondences for all entities in a map, which is fused with a Bayes filter to create a time series of pose estimates. The method generalizes across location, lighting, weather, and other challenges, and code and datasets are available.
